q: A Client wants to know the exact total professional fee upfront before construction begins, and the scope of services (design, approvals, construction schedule) can already be clearly and fully defined at the outset. Which method of compensation should the Architect propose?
o: Percentage-based Fee on PCC
Lump Sum or Fixed Fee
Multiple of Direct Personnel Expense
Per Diem, Honorarium plus Reimbursable Expenses
n: Lump Sum fits when scope, schedule, and approvals are already fully defined, letting both parties fix the total fee in advance. [Source: Sec. 4.2.1, UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210]

q: A Client wants a single point of responsibility for both the architectural design and the normal basic engineering works (structural, plumbing, sanitary, mechanical, electrical). Under which contract arrangement should the Architect be engaged?
o: Detailed Architectural Design Services (DADS)
Comprehensive Architectural Services
Detailed Architectural and Engineering Design Services (DAEDS)
Design-Build Services by Administration
n: DAEDS bundles architectural design with basic engineering under one contract, giving the Client a single point of responsibility. [Source: Sec. 4.1.1.3, UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210]

q: An Architect is asked to design the interior renovation of an existing office space, using a similar historical project's cost per square meter as reference. Compared to a new-build project of the same unit cost, how should the Architect treat the required service effort?
o: Apply the same effort since unit cost method standardizes all projects equally
Reduce the fee since renovation reuses existing structural elements
Recognize that renovation work requires greater service effort per unit than new work
Convert the project to a Lump Sum arrangement instead
n: The Guidelines explicitly note that renovation work demands more service effort per unit area than comparable new construction. [Source: Sec. 4.1.2, UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210]

q: A Client needs the Architect to serve as an expert witness in a construction-related court case — a short, interim engagement that is difficult to scope in advance. Which method of compensation is most appropriate?
o: Percentage of Gross Rentals
Unit Cost Method
Time Basis (hourly/per diem)
Value-based Pricing
n: Time Basis fits engagements that are short, interim, or hard to scope in advance, such as expert-witness testimony. [Source: Sec. 4.3.1–4.3.2, UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210]

q: A Client wants an Architect available for consultation at intervals over the coming year, without engaging the Architect full-time, and is willing to pay a stipulated amount regularly for a minimum service obligation. What compensation arrangement fits this situation?
o: Multiple of Direct Personnel Expense
Retainer
Lump Sum or Fixed Fee
Value-based Pricing / Percentage of Gross Rentals
n: A Retainer is used precisely for on-call, interval-based engagements paid a regular stipulated amount for a minimum service obligation. [Source: Sec. 4.3.13, UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210]

q: An Architect's office is tasked with purely administrative work for a project — record-keeping, data-gathering, and report preparation, with no creative-design input involved. Why is the Multiple of Direct Personnel Expense method specifically suited to this task?
o: It is the default method for all architectural services regardless of nature
It applies only to services requiring a licensed engineer
It applies only to non-creative work, since creative-design value cannot be measured by time spent
It guarantees the highest possible fee for the Architect
n: Multiple of DPE is reserved for non-creative work because time spent cannot fairly measure the value of creative design. [Source: Sec. 4.3.8, UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210]

q: For a single project, an Architect is asked to prepare architectural renderings for marketing purposes (a clearly determinate, specific service) while also providing ongoing design services for the rest of the project. How should the Architect structure the compensation for these two components?
o: Charge both components using only a percentage of PCC
Charge the rendering at a fixed price/lump sum, while the other services are compensated on a per diem or % of construction cost basis (Mixed Methods)
Refuse the rendering request since it falls outside the SPP
Charge both components purely on an hourly basis
n: Mixed Methods lets a determinate service be billed as a fixed price while other, less-determinate services use a different basis. [Source: Sec. 4.4.1, UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210]

q: A Client commissions an Architect to design a public market with minimal architectural finishes and simple engineering requirements. Under the Schedule of Fees, how should this project be classified?
o: Group 3 — Exceptional character/complexity
Group 1 — Simplest utilization/character
Group 5 — Monumental buildings
Group 8 — Extensive detail
n: Group 1 covers buildings with the simplest utilization/character and minimum finishes, such as public markets. [Source: Sec. 6.3, Group 1, UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210]

q: An Architect is engaged to renovate and expand an existing school building (originally classified under Group 2). How should the Recommended Professional Fee be adjusted for this engagement?
o: The RPF remains unchanged since it is the same building type
The RPF is reduced by 50% since existing structural work is reused
The RPF is increased by 50%, i.e., a total of 150% of the applicable RPF for Group 9 (alterations/renovations)
The RPF is computed solely on a Time Basis
n: Group 9 (alterations/renovations) adds 50% to the applicable RPF of the original building group, for a total of 150%. [Source: Sec. 6.3, Group 9, UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210]

q: The Architect has completed the Detailed Design and Contract Documents Phase (90% of the total work), but the Owner subsequently decides not to proceed with implementing the plans. What is the Architect entitled to receive?
o: Only the fee for the Schematic Design Phase
90% of the total Professional Fee
The full 100% Professional Fee regardless of completion
No fee, since the project did not proceed to construction
n: Once the Contract Documents Phase (90% of work) is done, the Architect keeps 90% of the fee even if the Owner abandons the project. [Source: Sec. 6.4.9, UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210]

q: Due to unforeseen circumstances, the Construction Phase of a project is suspended for eight (8) months. How should the fee for the remaining Periodic Construction Supervision works be treated once work resumes?
o: It remains the same as originally agreed
It is reduced by half to account for the delay
It is doubled, since the suspension exceeded six (6) months
It is converted automatically to a Lump Sum arrangement
n: A construction suspension beyond six months doubles the fee for the remaining Periodic Construction Supervision work. [Source: Sec. 6.4.10, UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210]

q: A Client decides to hire a Specialist Consultant (SC) directly and separately, rather than through the Architect, but still expects the Architect-of-Record to coordinate the SC's work with the overall design. What compensation is the Architect entitled to for this coordination work?
o: No additional compensation, since coordination is part of the basic fee
A coordination fee equivalent to 5% of the Specialist Consultant's fee
50% of the Specialist Consultant's fee
A fee equal to the SC's fee, paid by the Client
n: When a Client engages a Specialist Consultant directly, the Architect-of-Record still earns a 5% coordination fee on the SC's fee. [Source: Sec. 7.2.3 / Sec. 8.5, UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210]

q: A dispute arises between an Architect and Client over the Service Agreement. The parties attempt direct negotiation for 14 calendar days but fail to reach a resolution. What is the appropriate next step before initiating formal arbitration?
o: Immediately file a case in a regular court
Either party may initiate mediation/conciliatory discussions with a neutral third party within another 14 days
The Architect must unilaterally terminate the Service Agreement
Wait indefinitely until the Client agrees to arbitration
n: Sec. 19.2 sequences dispute resolution: negotiation first, then mediation with a neutral third party, before formal arbitration. [Source: Sec. 19.2, UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210]

q: An Owner fails to pay the Architect's billed fees within thirty (30) days from receipt of the statement of account, with no dispute over the amount owed. What is the Architect entitled to under the Guidelines?
o: Nothing, since fees are due only upon project completion
Interest at the prevailing rate set by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), as mutually agreed with the Client
Automatic termination of the Service Agreement
A penalty equal to 50% of the unpaid amount
n: Sec. 16 entitles the Architect to interest at the BSP rate on fees unpaid 30 days after billing, as agreed with the Client. [Source: Sec. 16, UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210]

q: An unlicensed and unregistered individual collects payment for architectural design services rendered on a residential project. Under this Guideline, how is this act characterized?
o: Permissible, provided the Client consents in writing
Permissible only for Group 4 (residential) projects
Unlawful, as provided under R.A. 9266
Permissible if a licensed Architect later reviews the work
n: R.A. 9266 makes it unlawful for anyone without a valid license/registration to collect fees for architectural services. [Source: Sec. 15, UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210]
